title: Why our merges wait in line on a free GitHub account

params.title: Why our merges wait in line

spoken.said: This is an open question, not an explainer. Two repositories, one person, and a crowd of agent sessions all merge into GitHub on a free personal account, and the merges wait in line. I'll show where the time goes, with the numbers, what we settled on, and why we still don't like it. If you know a better pattern that stays on GitHub and costs nothing, that's the part I'm asking for. It's as of November twenty-fourth, twenty twenty-six, and the pages you'll see were photographed that day; the numbers were measured on November twenty-first.

sources.quote: The evidence behind the open-question essay on merges

spoken.narration: Start with one small pull request, merged on November twenty-first. It adds three records of decisions and one entry to a ledger. Four JSON files, sixty-one lines, and no code at all.

sources.quote: "docs/calls/C1013.json","docs/calls/C1014.json","docs/calls/C1015.json","packages/assurance/src/ledger.json"

spoken.narration: Its main workflow ran for fifteen and a half minutes of wall time, and its checks spent thirty-three runner-minutes in all. The Rust build and tests, and five Rust dependency checks, all ran and all passed. The pull request touched no Rust, so none of them could have failed.

spoken.narration: The job that decides what runs logged why. A filter called rust matched every one of the four files. GitHub shows this log only to people who sign in, so these lines are copied from it, word for word.

params.title: A negation, read as one more way to match

spoken.narration: Here is the cause. The Rust and Node lists each ended with a pattern meant to leave Markdown out. But the filter's default rule is that a file counts when any one pattern matches it, and 'not Markdown' matches nearly every file there is. So the Rust flag and the Node flag were on for almost every pull request. That pattern has since been fixed, and a check now refuses it.

spoken.narration: Over the last thirty merged pull requests, that's a thousand of three thousand eight hundred runner-minutes, about a quarter, spent on jobs the change could not fail. Most of it is the Rust dependency checks, on twenty-eight pull requests that had no Rust in them.

spoken.narration: Another pull request that evening changed one test fixture and spent eighty-six minutes. Seventeen of them couldn't fail. Thirty-nine more were the whole suite run again, because another branch had merged first and this one had to catch up.

params.title: A merge of main, then every PR runs again

spoken.narration: Catching up is the bigger cost. Both repositories require a branch to be up to date before it merges. So each merge puts every open pull request behind, and each one runs its whole suite again with no change of its own. On one day, that was thirty-eight percent of the minutes here, and sixteen percent on the server.

sources.quote: update-branch reruns were

spoken.narration: In the list of runs it looks like this. A later pull request's branch, on November twenty-first: twelve runs from four pushes. Three were its author's own fixes. The fourth carried nothing of its own, only a merge of main, so it could catch up, and it ran the whole suite again. And through that day, CI found no fault that review had missed.

sources.quote: while CI found no fault review had missed on Nov 21
since the unfiltered list is live

spoken.narration: The tool built for this is GitHub's merge queue. It gives the same safety as up to date, without making each author re-run. GitHub's own page says who gets it: public repositories owned by an organization, or private ones on Enterprise Cloud. Ours belong to a personal account, so it isn't offered to us.

spoken.narration: So the answer has to keep four things. It stays on GitHub. It costs nothing. Main never goes red because two green branches met for the first time after merging. And CI stays, because it is what makes drift loud, even on the days it finds nothing.

params.title: Settle every branch, then land them together

steps.label: Settle
steps.note: Review, fixes and local checks, before any PR

steps.label: Bucket
steps.note: One to seven settled branches in one PR

steps.label: One CI round
steps.note: Instead of one per branch, per merge

spoken.narration: What we settled on has two parts. First, a branch does all its settling before it ever opens a pull request: review, fixes, and the checks a laptop can run. Then one to seven settled branches land together in one bucket, so one CI round covers all of them. Second, fix the filter, so a change only runs the jobs it can fail.

spoken.narration: Buckets trade one pain for others. A single flaky test now holds back several branches, not one. Reverting a feature means picking it back out of a bucket. Changes that come in pairs across the two repositories still go one after the other. And both repositories share one pool of runners, so under load the queue never clears.

params.title: Is there a better pattern, free, on GitHub?

rows.note: move the repos to a free organization: the queue is offered there
a bot branch that tests a batch once, then fast-forwards main
loose gate on the PR, full suite on main, revert on red
the one we haven't thought of

spoken.narration: Here's where I'd like help. A free organization seems to get the merge queue on public repositories, so moving there might be the whole answer, if nothing else breaks. Or a train: a bot branch that tests a batch once and then fast-forwards main. Or a looser gate on the pull request, the full suite on main, and a revert when it goes red. Each one gives something up. Which would you pick, or what are we missing?
